Q33. First law: The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal at the point of incidence, all lie in the same plane.
Second law (Snell's Law): The ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is a constant for a given pair of media and a given colour of light. i.e., sin i / sin r = constant = µ.

Q34. The refractive index of a medium is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum (or air) to the speed of light in that medium. It is given by µ = c/v, where c is the speed of light in vacuum and v is the speed of light in the medium. Refractive index has no unit (it is a dimensionless quantity).

Q35. Apparent depth is the depth at which an object submerged in a denser medium appears to be when viewed from a rarer medium (e.g., air). It is less than the real depth because refraction causes the rays to bend away from the normal as they leave the denser medium, making the object appear closer. Real depth is the actual distance of the object below the surface.

(iii) Refractive index of the material — higher refractive index, greater lateral displacement.

Q42. Two factors:
(i) Colour (wavelength) of light: Violet light has the highest refractive index, so it has the smallest critical angle. Red light has the lowest refractive index and therefore the largest critical angle among visible colours.
(ii) Temperature: As temperature increases, the refractive index of the medium decreases (medium expands, density decreases, speed of light increases). Therefore, the critical angle increases with rise in temperature.

Q44. (a) Lowest critical angle: Diamond (µ = 2.41; sin C = 1/2.41; C ≈ 24.4°).
Highest critical angle: Water (µ = 1.33; sin C = 1/1.33; C ≈ 48.8°).
(b) When temperature is raised, the refractive index of each substance decreases (density decreases, speed of light increases). Since sin C = 1/µ, a decrease in µ means sin C increases, so the critical angle increases for all substances.

Q45. Reflection from a plane mirror: Only about 95% of the incident light is reflected; some light is absorbed by the mirror surface and some is transmitted through the glass. The image is slightly dim.
Total internal reflection from a prism: 100% of the incident light is reflected; there is no absorption or transmission. The image is much brighter and clearer.
(Other valid differences: A plane mirror may lose its reflecting property over time due to tarnishing of the silver coating, while a TIR prism retains its property indefinitely.)

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q46. This is due to the phenomenon of mirage caused by total internal reflection. On a hot summer day, the air near the ground becomes very hot and less dense, while the air higher up is cooler and denser. Light from the trees and houses travels from denser (cooler, upper) layers to rarer (hotter, lower) layers. The refractive index gradually decreases downwards, causing continuous refraction. When the angle of incidence in the lower hot layer exceeds the critical angle, TIR occurs, producing an inverted image of the objects. The fluctuating air makes the image appear to shake.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q47. Stars near the horizon: Light from these stars travels a much longer path through the atmosphere and passes through many layers of air of varying refractive indices and temperatures. The continuous refraction and shifting of the apparent position of the star as air currents move cause the star's light to fluctuate in intensity and direction, making the star appear to twinkle.
Stars overhead: Light from stars overhead travels a shorter, more vertical path through the atmosphere. There are fewer refractions and the layers are relatively uniform directly overhead, so the apparent position does not shift significantly, and the stars do not appear to twinkle.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q48. Normal reflection | Total internal reflection
(i) Occurs at any angle of incidence. | Occurs only when angle of incidence > critical angle.
(ii) Only about 95% of light is reflected; some is absorbed or transmitted. | 100% of light is reflected; no energy loss.
(iii) Can occur when light travels from any medium to any other. | Occurs only when light travels from a denser to a rarer medium.
(iv) Occurs at polished surfaces (mirrors). | Occurs at the interface of a denser and rarer medium.

D. Long Answer Questions

Q59. Critical angle is defined as the angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction in the rarer medium is exactly 90°.

Explanation with diagram:
Consider a ray of light passing from glass (denser) to air (rarer). As the angle of incidence i is increased:
• When i < C: the ray refracts into air, bending away from the normal.
• When i = C: the refracted ray just grazes along the glass-air surface (angle of refraction = 90°). This angle i = C is the critical angle.
• When i > C: no refraction occurs; the ray is totally reflected back into the glass (TIR).

Mathematical relation: sin C = 1/µ (where µ is the refractive index of glass w.r.t. air).

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q60. (a) Total internal reflection (TIR): When a ray of light travels from a denser medium to a rarer medium and the angle of incidence in the denser medium exceeds the critical angle for that pair of media, the ray is completely reflected back into the denser medium. This phenomenon is called total internal reflection.

(b) Conditions for TIR:
(i) Light must travel from a denser medium to a rarer medium (e.g., glass to air, water to air).
(ii) The angle of incidence in the denser medium must be greater than the critical angle for that pair of media.

(c) Diagram: A point source P inside a glass block. Rays from P hit the glass-air interface at various angles:
— Ray at i < C: partly refracted, partly reflected.
— Ray at i = C: refracted along interface (90°).
— Ray at i > C: completely reflected back into glass (TIR).

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q61. (a) Path of rays after striking the water surface:
— Ray A (angle of incidence < 48°): undergoes refraction; bends away from normal as it enters air.
— Ray B (angle of incidence = 48°): refracted at exactly 90° along the water surface.
— Ray C (angle of incidence > 48°): undergoes total internal reflection; angle of reflection equals angle of incidence.

(b) Phenomena:
— Ray A: Refraction (partial refraction and partial reflection).
— Ray B: Grazing refraction / the critical angle condition.
— Ray C: Total internal reflection.

Q62. A total reflecting prism is a right-angled isosceles prism (with angles 45°, 45° and 90°) that uses total internal reflection to reflect light. Since the critical angle for glass is about 42°, a ray hitting any of its faces at 45° (> 42°) undergoes TIR.

Three actions of a total reflecting prism:
(i) It can turn a ray of light through 90° (used in periscopes and binoculars).
(ii) It can turn a ray of light through 180° (used in binoculars to invert the image).
(iii) It can invert an image without changing its left-right orientation (used in image erecting systems in telescopes).

Diagram (turning ray through 90°): A right-angled isosceles prism with the right angle at top. A horizontal ray enters the vertical face normally, strikes the hypotenuse at 45° (TIR occurs), and exits the horizontal face vertically downward.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q63. A right-angled isosceles prism (45°-45°-90°) can turn a ray of light through 90° as follows:

The ray XY enters one face of the prism normally (perpendicularly), so it passes through without any deviation. It then strikes the hypotenuse face at an angle of incidence of 45°. Since the critical angle for glass is about 42°, the condition for TIR (i > C) is satisfied. The ray undergoes total internal reflection at the hypotenuse and emerges from the other face at right angles to its original direction — turned through 90°.

Instrument: Periscope. A periscope uses two such prisms to allow an observer to see over obstacles.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q64. (a) The incident ray XY deviates through 90°. The ray enters one face normally, strikes the hypotenuse at 45° (TIR occurs), and exits through the other face — turned by 90°.
(b) Periscope (or binoculars).
(c) The hypotenuse face (the longest face at 45° to the other two) behaves as the mirror — this is the surface at which total internal reflection takes place.

Official Answer

Q65. A right-angled isosceles prism (45°-45°-90°) can erect an inverted image by turning the image through 180° using two total internal reflections.

The inverted image acts as the object. Light rays from it enter the hypotenuse face of the prism normally. They strike the first 45° face and undergo TIR, travel across the prism, strike the second 45° face and undergo TIR again. The rays then exit through the hypotenuse. The image is now rotated 180° and appears erect.

This prism is used in binoculars and in Galilean telescopes as an image erector.

Official Answer

Q66. (a) At face AB: angle of incidence = 0° (ray enters normally).
At face AC: angle of incidence = 60° (equals the critical angle for equilateral prism; ray inside makes 60° with the normal to AC).
At face BC: the ray exits by refraction.

(b) At face AB — Refraction (enters normally, no bending, i = 0°).
At face AC — Total internal reflection (i = 60° > critical angle 42°); ray reflects at 60°.
At face BC — Refraction (ray exits from the denser glass into air).

Official Answer

Q67. (a) Ray PQ enters normally through the hypotenuse (no refraction, goes straight). It strikes the first 45° face at 45° (> critical angle 42°), undergoes TIR. It then crosses to the second 45° face at 45°, undergoes TIR again. Finally it exits through the hypotenuse going in the opposite direction to the original.

(b) Angle of deviation = 180°. The emergent ray is antiparallel (opposite direction) to the incident ray.

(c) Binoculars (or a retroreflector used in rangefinders).

Official Answer

Q68. A right-angled isosceles prism (total reflecting prism) can turn a ray of light through 180°.

How it works: The ray enters normally through the hypotenuse, strikes the first 45° face at 45° (> critical angle), undergoes TIR, travels across to the second 45° face, undergoes TIR again, and exits from the hypotenuse parallel but opposite to its original direction — a deviation of 180°.

Instrument: Binoculars use two such prisms (Porro prism system) to erect and shorten the image path.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q69. In prism P: The ray enters the vertical face normally (no refraction). It travels horizontally and hits the hypotenuse at 45° (TIR, since 45° > critical angle 42°). The ray is turned down by 90° and exits through the bottom horizontal face without bending (normal incidence).

In prism Q (inverted below P or alongside): The ray enters the horizontal face of prism Q normally. It travels and strikes the hypotenuse at 45° (TIR again). The ray is turned and exits through the other face. The combined effect of two TIRs inverts the ray — used in the Porro prism binocular system to erect the image.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q70. A right-angled isosceles prism used with the hypotenuse at the top and light rays falling normally on the hypotenuse will invert the image (flip top-to-bottom) without affecting the left-right sense.

Description of ray path:
(i) Two parallel rays fall perpendicularly on the hypotenuse face and enter without bending.
(ii) Each ray strikes the first 45° face at 45° — TIR occurs (45° > 42° critical angle), ray deflects downward.
(iii) The ray strikes the second 45° face at 45° — TIR occurs again, ray exits through the hypotenuse going in a direction parallel but laterally shifted from the original path.
(iv) The top ray and bottom ray exchange positions, inverting the image.

The image is upright but inverted (the object's top becomes the bottom), with no left-right reversal. This action is used in image-erecting systems of telescopes.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q71. Mirage is an optical illusion in which a pool of water appears to be seen on the road or desert during hot summer days.

Cause — Total internal reflection:
(i) On a hot day, the air near the ground is very hot and hence less dense (lower refractive index). The layers of air get progressively cooler and denser (higher refractive index) as we go higher.
(ii) A ray of light from the top of a tree or the sky travels obliquely downward through these layers of decreasing refractive index, continuously bending away from the normal at each layer.
(iii) Eventually, when the angle of incidence in a lower hot layer exceeds the critical angle for that layer, total internal reflection occurs.
(iv) The TIR ray then travels upward through progressively denser layers, again refracting and eventually reaching the observer's eye.
(v) The observer sees a shimmering, inverted image of the sky or tree near the ground level, which looks like a pool of water.

Diagram: Shows tree, multiple air layers with decreasing density near ground, curved ray path from tree top bending downward and then upward after TIR, reaching eye of observer.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q72. Working of optical fibres:
An optical fibre is a thin, flexible strand of glass or plastic with a high refractive index core surrounded by a cladding of lower refractive index.

(i) Light is introduced at one end of the fibre at a small angle to the axis.
(ii) The light hits the core-cladding interface at an angle greater than the critical angle.
(iii) Total internal reflection occurs, and the light bounces along the fibre, reflecting repeatedly off the walls without loss of energy.
(iv) Light travels through thousands of such reflections and emerges from the other end with almost no loss of intensity, regardless of how the fibre is bent.

Application:
(i) Endoscopy — optical fibres are used in endoscopes to view internal organs of the human body without surgery.
(ii) Telecommunications — optical fibres carry telephone, internet, and television signals as pulses of light over long distances with minimal signal loss.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q77. (a) Speed of light in vacuum = 10x/t₁.
In diamond (µ ≈ 2.41), speed is less than in vacuum, so distance covered in time t₁ would be less than 10x. The statement is FALSE.

(b) Speed in vacuum: c = 10x/t₁
Speed in medium: v = x/t₂
µ = c/v = (10x/t₁) ÷ (x/t₂) = (10x/t₁) × (t₂/x) = 10t₂/t₁.
Refractive index of the medium = 10t₂/t₁.

The critical angle for glass-air interface is approximately 42°.

Q80. Given: Critical angle C = 60°; angle DE makes 150° with AC; angle EDB = 90°.

Inside the prism, at point E on face AC: the angle between DE and AC is (180° − 150°) = 30°. Normal to AC is perpendicular to AC, so angle of incidence at E = 90° − 30° = 60°.

Since the angle of incidence at E = 60° = critical angle, the ray DE is refracted at 90° (grazes along EC at the surface).
The refracted ray at E travels along the surface AC (angle of refraction = 90°).

At point D on face AB: The ray enters normally (i = 0°), so it passes undeviated into the prism.

Result: The ray emerges along the surface AC (grazing the surface); angle of emergence = 90°.

Official Answer

Q81. (a) Real depth = 25 cm; µ = 1.25.
Apparent depth = Real depth / µ = 25/1.25 = 20 cm.
The ruler will get wet up to the 20 cm mark.

(b) If µ > 1.25, the apparent depth = Real depth/µ would be less than 20 cm (since dividing by a larger number gives a smaller result). So the ruler would get wet up to a mark less than 20 cm — the apparent depth decreases.

Q82. sin C = 1/µ = 1/2.41 = 0.4149
C = sin⁻¹(0.4149) = 24.4° ≈ 24°.
The critical angle for the diamond-air interface is approximately 24°.

Q83. (a) At minimum deviation, the ray travels symmetrically through the prism. For an equilateral prism (A = 60°), the angle of refraction at the first surface = A/2 = 60°/2 = 30°.

(b) Applying Snell's law at the first surface (light going from air to glass):
µ = sin(i)/sin(r) = sin(45°)/sin(30°) = (√2/2)/(1/2) = (√2/2) × 2 = √2 ≈ 1.414.
The refractive index of the prism material is √2 ≈ 1.41.

(b) µ = c/v → v = c/µ = (3 × 10⁸)/1.462 = 2.05 × 10⁸ ms⁻¹.

Q86. (a) Since the ray just grazes along the exit face (angle of refraction = 90°), the angle of incidence at that face equals the critical angle. From the prism geometry, the critical angle = 45°.
Sin C = 1/µ → µ = 1/sin 45° = 1/(√2/2) = √2 ≈ 1.414.
Critical angle for blue colour ≈ 45°.

(b) For a right-angled prism where the ray enters one face and undergoes critical angle condition at the hypotenuse, the apex angle A = 45°. The prism is a right-angled isosceles prism (45°-45°-90°), so the angle A at the relevant apex = 45°.

(c) Violet light has a higher refractive index than blue, so a lower critical angle than blue. The violet ray would undergo TIR at the same surface where blue just grazes (since its critical angle < 45°). Therefore, violet (or any colour with higher refractive index than blue) should replace the blue ray.

Official Answer

Q87. By Snell's law: sin i / sin r = µ_water
sin r = sin i / µ = sin 45° / (4/3) = 0.707 / 1.333 = 0.530
r = sin⁻¹(0.530) = 32°.
The angle of refraction in water is approximately 32°.
